title: Tourism Secretary Chairs Industry Talks on India's Travel Sector Woes
excerpt: Bhuvnesh Kumar’s consultation with the travel trade comes as the ministry pushes ease-of-doing-business reforms and presses the industry to spread demand beyond overcrowded hotspots.
body:
• Tourism Secretary Bhuvnesh Kumar has chaired an industry consultation on the on-ground challenges facing India's travel and tourism sector — the latest in a series of ministry-industry dialogues on regulation, visas and investment.
  • The trade's recurring demands: easier visa facilitation, rationalised taxation, faster investment approvals and simpler licensing — with industry warning that fragmented state-level rules and slow clearances hurt competitiveness.
  • The ministry's reform agenda includes delinking hotel licences from its classification system, moving classification from inspection-based assessment to self-declaration, and phased reduction of checklist requirements.
  • For travellers: India's e-visa now covers 171 countries and visa categories have been cut from 22 to nine; under Dekho Apna Desh 2.0, expect the ministry to push lesser-known destinations such as Turtuk, Gurez, Doodhpatri and Varkala to spread demand.

Tourism Secretary Bhuvnesh Kumar has convened the travel industry for a consultation on the challenges facing India's tourism sector, as the Ministry of Tourism presses ahead with its ease-of-doing-business reforms and tries to convert the country's post-pandemic travel boom into durable, high-quality growth.

What the industry is asking for

The consultation continues a running conversation between the ministry and the trade. In earlier sessions this year, industry representatives — from bodies including FAITH, ASSOCHAM, CII and the Indian Association of Tour Operators — raised a consistent set of complaints: visa facilitation, taxation, investment approvals and licensing timelines. Stakeholders stressed the need for closer coordination between central ministries, state governments and Union Territories to speed up implementation, warning that India must stay globally competitive to attract investment.

On the ground, the grievances are concrete. Tour operators cite inadequate amenities at destinations, crowd management failures, guide shortages, sudden fee hikes at monuments, and a regulatory maze that makes it easier to add hotel capacity abroad than at home. The ministry, for its part, has presented its reform agenda as an answer: the delinking of licences from the ministry's classification system for hospitality establishments has already begun.

The reform agenda on the table

Secretary Kumar has proposed moving hotel classification from inspection-based assessments to a self-declaration model, with checklist requirements and mandatory certifications reduced through a phased, time-bound approach. Industry representatives welcomed the proposal as a direct reduction of compliance burden.

The ministry is also building longer-term digital infrastructure. The National Digital Tourism Stack, being developed with ONDC, aims to make tourism offerings discoverable and trustworthy through verified identities, ratings and grievance redressal — with a pilot planned for January 2027. Alongside it, the National Mission for Alternative Destinations, or Dekho Apna Desh 2.0, seeks to redistribute demand from overcrowded hubs to tourism-ready but lesser-known destinations.

"We don't really need more domestic tourism. We need distributed demand."

— Bhuvnesh Kumar, Tourism Secretary

The bigger picture: booming at home, losing abroad

The consultation comes against an uncomfortable arithmetic. India was net positive on travel foreign exchange until about 2021; it is now net negative, with Indians spending more abroad than foreign visitors spend at home. Additional Secretary Suman Billa has warned that outbound travel is growing at 4.8%, far faster than inbound — and that new aviation connectivity is a double-edged sword: it makes it as easy to leave India as to enter it.

Domestic numbers, meanwhile, mask the gap. Domestic visits reached 429 crore last year, and organised hotel room supply has more than doubled in a decade — from 80,000 to 200,000 classified rooms. The government believes even that falls short of demand, and the risk is complacency: a sector comfortable with its domestic market can neglect the harder work of winning international visitors.

Diaspora angle

For NRIs, the consultation's outcomes matter at trip-planning level. The visa reforms already delivered — categories cut from 22 to nine, e-visa now covering 171 countries — have simplified visits home. And with Diwali travel demand already pushing festive-season airfares up, the ministry's push to distribute demand means more bookable itineraries beyond the usual circuits, which is exactly where diaspora visitors tend to want to go.

What's next

The test of the consultation is implementation: whether self-declaration classification and a genuinely single-window system move from proposal to phased rollout, and whether the January 2027 Digital Tourism Stack pilot gives travellers and operators something they can actually use. The ministry has set the direction; the industry will be watching the calendar.
